content: 1. The study by Smeets (2008) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to the absence of follow-up scores, despite providing within-group mean changes. It involved 119 participants and was rated as having an overall low risk of bias. Participants underwent a combination treatment consisting of active physical exercises (aerobic and core strengthening) and graded activity with problem-solving training, compared to graded activity with problem-solving training alone. 2. Dalichau (2003) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study, involving 90 participants, was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It compared mixed exercise interventions to no treatment or no additional treatment. The authors reported greater improvements in disability in the exercise group, although the effect estimates were unclear. 3. McIlveen (1998) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study included 95 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. The outcomes were measured using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) on a 0–100 scale. 4. Kanwal (2021) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study involved 24 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It compared core strengthening exercises to no treatment or no additional treatment. 5. Raza (2020) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study included 40 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It investigated stretching or flexibility/mobilizing exercises. No significant differences were observed for individual items on the ODI (0–5 scale). 6. Da Silva (2014) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study involved 18 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It examined mixed exercise interventions, with benefits indicated by lower scores on the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ, 0–24 scale). 7. Wattamwar (2012) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study included 24 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It focused on yoga exercises. 8. Sedaghati (2017) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study involved 34 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It examined mixed exercises (both in and out of water) and stretching or flexibility/mobilizing exercises. No significant differences were found in follow-up scores between the stretching/flexibility group and the no-treatment group, as measured by the Quebec Back Pain Disability Scale (0–100 scale). 9. Liu (2018) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study included 43 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias. It investigated Tai Chi and core strengthening exercises. The authors reported significant reductions in the average ODI scores in each domain for both exercise groups compared to the comparison group, although overall scores were not reported (ODI 0–50 scale). 10. Rathi (2013) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. This study involved 30 participants and was rated as having a high overall risk of bias.
